summary: This article explains how illustrators draw pictures that go with written stories, how illustration differs from fine art, and how pictures have helped tell stories in books for a very long time.
introduce: Draw two overlapping circles on the board and quickly compare two familiar things, such as a cat and a dog, with the class. Tell students that while reading “Illustration: Telling Stories with Pictures” they will look for ways things are alike and different.

keyTerms.def: to arrange the parts of a picture in a careful, planned way
the group of people who read, watch, or look at something
very clear, bright, and easy to picture in your mind

challengeTerms.def: a story, or the way a story is told
to go well with something and make it better or more complete
the range of colors an artist chooses to use in a piece of work

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that a picture can tell part of a story just as well as words can? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Explain how illustration is different from fine art, and why that difference matters for a children's book.
struggling: Read the first part of the article aloud together, review compose, audience, and vivid, and let weak readers fill in a T-chart of alike and different with sentence starters.
gifted: Challenge advanced readers to use narrative, complement, and palette in a short paragraph that compares two ideas from the article and explain which difference matters most.
